items.title: MSR-HuBERT: Self-supervised Pre-training for Adaptation to Multiple Sampling Rates
items.authors: Zikang Huang(Tianjin University); Meng Ge(Tianjin University); Tianrui Wang(Tianjin University); Xuanchen Li(Tianjin University); Xiaobao Wang(Tianjin University); Longbiao Wang(Tianjin Key Laboratory of Cognitive ComputTianjin University; Huiyan Technology Company, Ltd.); Jianwu Dang(Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology)
items.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has advanced speech processing. However, existing speech SSL methods typically assume a single sampling rate and struggle with mixed-rate data due to temporal resolution mismatch. To address this limitation, we propose MSRHuBERT, a multi-sampling-rate adaptive pre-training method. Building on HuBERT, we replace its single-rate downsampling CNN with a multi-sampling-rate adaptive downsampling CNN that maps raw waveforms from different sampling rates to a shared temporal resolution without resampling. This design enables unified mixed-rate pre-training and fine-tuning. In experiments spanning 16 to 48 kHz, MSRHuBERT outperforms HuBERT on speech recognition and full-band speech reconstruction, preserving high-frequency detail while modeling low-frequency semantic structure. Moreover, MSRHuBERT retains HuBERT's mask-prediction objective and Transformer encoder, so existing analyses and improvements that were developed for HuBERT can apply directly.

items.title: Online Predictive Coding for Dual-Mode Self-Supervised Speech Models
items.authors: Keita Goto(LY Corporation); Takashi Maekaku(LY Corporation); Jin Sakuma(LY Corporation); Jinchuan Tian(Carnegie Mellon University); Yusuke Shinohara(LY Corporation); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University)
items.abstract: Dual-mode self-supervised speech models are pre-trained to handle streaming and non-streaming conditions simultaneously. However, their attention is computed over different context ranges, which often makes optimization difficult. In previous work, we proposed online registers, additional tokens intended to compensate for missing future context in streaming mode, but the gains remained limited. To address these issues, we introduce two improvements for robust dual-mode pre-training: (1) Online Predictive Coding (OPC), which regularizes the registers through multi-step future prediction, and (2) Dual-mode Layer Normalization, which stabilizes optimization. We fine-tune the proposed dual-mode self-supervised speech models for speech recognition on LibriSpeech and WSJ. Results show that OPC consistently reduces the online-offline performance gap; at 160 ms latency on LibriSpeech, word error rates improve from 3.65% to 3.40% on test-clean and from 10.15% to 9.65% on test-other.

items.title: Enhancing BEST-RQ Pseudo-Label Quality Through Online Refinement for Automatic Speech Recognition
items.authors: Jingjing Xu(RWTH University; AppTek); Zijian Yang(RWTH University); Mohammad Zeineldeen(RWTH University; AppTek); Eugen Beck(AppTek); Ralf Schlüter(RWTH University; AppTek); Hermann Ney(RWTH University; AppTek)
items.abstract: BEST-RQ is a simple and effective self-supervised training method for speech representation learning that performs well on automatic speech recognition (ASR) tasks. It generates pseudolabels using a fixed online quantization scheme, which simplifies training but provides weaker supervision than HuBERT-style models that iteratively refine pseudo-labels. In this work, we improve online pseudo-label generation while preserving simplicity. We propose three modifications: replacing the quantizer's linear projection with Principal Component Analysis (PCA), updating the codebook via iterative codebook refinement and introducing an additional codebook updated via codebook distillation. We pre-train on the Librispeech 960-hour dataset and fine-tune using 100 hours of supervised Librispeech data. With all three modifications enabled, we achieve a 12% relative reduction in word error rate (WER) on the Librispeech test-other set, improving from 10.1% to 8.8%.

items.title: Pretrained self-supervised speech models can recognize unseen consonants
items.authors: Chihiro Taguchi(University of Notre Dame); Éric Le Ferrand(University at Buffalo); Hirosi Nakagawa(Tokyo University of Foreign Studies); Hitomi Ono(Reitaku University); Kanji Kato(Tokyo University of Foreign Studies); Emily Prud'hommeaux(Boston College); David Chiang(University of Notre Dame)
items.abstract: Modern pretrained self-supervised automatic speech recognition models are trained on large-scale audio data to encode speech into contextualized representations. However, their training data are heavily skewed toward high-resource languages with little data from low-resource languages, raising concerns about the potential underrepresentation of typologically uncommon speech sounds such as click consonants primarily found in Khoisan languages. This leads to our central research question: Can these models recognize click consonants as accurately as other speech sounds? To address this question, we fine-tune and compare pretrained self-supervised speech models (Wav2Vec2 and HuBERT) on data from two click-rich Khoisan languages (G|ui and West !Xoon). Our results reveal that the fine-tuned models consistently recognize clicks more accurately than non-clicks, suggesting that self-supervision enables generalization across human speech sounds including rare phonemes.

items.title: IACC-HuBERT: Intelligibility-Aware Channel Conditioning of HuBERT Frontend for Dysarthric Speech Conformer ASR
items.authors: Paban Sapkota(National Institute of Technology); Hemant Kumar Kathania(National Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: Recent speech foundation models have advanced automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems, particularly for clean or controlled speech. However, no foundation models are specifically designed to capture the characteristics of dysarthric speech, making adaptation of existing models necessary. A common approach is to utilize pretrained self-supervised learning (SSL) models to extract robust speech representations for ASR. In this work, we propose an efficient adaptation method that conditions self-supervised HuBERT features on speaker intelligibility using channel-wise modulation through FiLM-only and Gated-FiLM mechanisms. By training only 6.3M (FiLM) to 15.78M (Gated-FiLM) parameters, the proposed method achieves WERs of 21.3% and 21.0%, respectively, introducing intelligibility-aware channel modulation of HuBERT features in an end-to-end Conformer ASR system.

items.title: ZipCodec: Simple and Pretrained-Model-Free Speech Tokenizer via Flow-Matching
items.authors: Lingxuan Ye(Xiaomi Corp.); Han Zhu(Xiaomi Corp.); Liyong Guo(Xiaomi Corp.); Zengwei Yao(Xiaomi Corp.); Wei Kang(Xiaomi Corp.); Fangjun Kuang(Xiaomi Corp.); Zhifeng Han(Xiaomi Corp.); Long Lin(Xiaomi Corp.); Daniel Povey(Xiaomi Corp.)
items.abstract: Speech tokenizers serve as the critical interface for integrating continuous audio into large language models. However, most existing speech tokenizers require massive pretrained models or complex multi-stage training pipelines. To address this, we propose ZipCodec, a single-stage-trained, pretrained-model-free tokenizer that bypasses the need for heavy encoder architectures. By offloading acoustic reconstruction to a powerful Zipformer-based flow-matching decoder, ZipCodec enables an ultra-lightweight encoder of just 4.4M parameters. Furthermore, we introduce an Encoder Consistency Regularization (ECR) loss to enhance the encoder's semantic capacity in a purely self-supervised manner, without relying on external teachers or labels. Experimental results demonstrate that ZipCodec achieves competitive acoustic and semantic performance, outperforming models with encoders more than 20 times larger and delivering improved zero-shot TTS generation.

items.title: Preserving Acoustic Cues for Video Reasoning: An Efficient Uniqueness-Driven Token Compression Framework
items.authors: Haiwei Xue(Tsinghua University; The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology); Zichao Nie(Tsinghua University); Zhiyong Wu(Tsinghua University; The Chinese University of Hong Kong)
items.abstract: Effective video reasoning requires the joint understanding of visual and acoustic cues. However, existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) either discard audio entirely or rely solely on ASR transcripts, forfeiting rich acoustic features such as prosody, environmental sounds, and speaker characteristics. Naively forwarding all audio tokens to an MLLM incurs prohibitive computational overhead. We propose Flash-VAReason, a framework that integrates efficient audio token compression into video reasoning via a three-stage pipeline grounded in information uniqueness theory: Audio Time Fusion, Budget Control, and Spatial Dynamic Compression. By quantifying the acoustic distinctiveness of each token, our method reduces the audio token count by an order of magnitude while retaining the most informative cues, enabling joint visual-audio reasoning without sacrificing inference speed. More information is available on the Project page.

items.title: Do Machines Listen Like Humans? A Temporal Benchmark for Phonological Competition in End-to-End ASR
items.authors: Linkai Peng(University of Connecticut); Christian Brodbeck(McMaster University); Sahil Luthra(Stony Brook University); Kevin Brown(Oregon State University); Jay Rueckl(University of Connecticut); Monty Escabi(University of Connecticut); David Gow(Massachusetts General Hospital); James S. Magnuson(University of Connecticut; BCBL; Ikerbasque)
items.abstract: Human speech perception is incremental, with listeners activating and suppressing potential words in real time as they hear speech. Some researchers have explored using modern Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models as potential models of human speech recognition (HSR). Here we ask whether ASR models process speech with human-like incremental dynamics, focusing on the time course of lexical activation and phonological competition. We propose a benchmark to quantitatively compare the time course of HSR and ASR, using a point-wise comparison of internal model activation trajectories against human eyetracking data. We define metrics to trace word activation profiles across various architectures. Our results reveal a clear dissociation: Causal models successfully replicate the hallmark human pattern of early competition between onset competitors, and later, weaker competition between words that rhyme, whereas non-causal models with 'look-ahead' mechanisms fail to capture these temporal dynamics. These findings demonstrate that architectural constraints are critical for developing speech systems that process language in a human-like manner, and suggest caution is warranted in considering ASR or other large language models as models of human language processing.

items.title: From Continuous Speech to Subglottal Resonances: Automatic Signal Generation, Estimation, and Tracking Framework
items.authors: Chigozie Uzochukwu Udeogu(University of Maryland); Carol Espy-Wilson(University of Maryland)
items.abstract: Although studies have shown subglottal resonances (SGRs) to be relevant for various speech processing tasks, their integration into speech-based applications has been limited by the difficulty of acquiring them and the absence of automated estimation methods. In this study, we address this challenge by developing a framework that generates accelerometer signals that contains the subglottal signals directly from speech via a supervised multi-scale spectral learning approach. Additionally, we introduce a novel algorithm for automatically estimating and tracking SGRs from continuous speech. Our method achieved low RMSE values (approximately 30 Hz, 50 Hz, and 80 Hz for Sgr1, Sgr2, and Sgr3, respectively) thus, demonstrating its accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, experiments conducted on the TIMIT dataset show that the estimation error remains below 7 cm, highlighting the method's applicability to real world applications.

items.title: Prosodic ABX: A Language-Agnostic Method for Measuring Prosodic Contrast in Speech Representations
items.authors: Haitong Sun(The University of Tokyo); Stephen McIntosh(The University of Tokyo); Kwanghee Choi(University of Texas at Austin); Eunjung Yeo(University of Texas at Austin); Daisuke Saito(The University of Tokyo); Nobuaki Minematsu(The University of Tokyo)
items.abstract: Speech representations from self-supervised speech models (S3Ms) are known to be sensitive to phonemic contrasts, but their sensitivity to prosodic contrasts has not been directly measured. The ABX discrimination task has been used to measure phonemic contrast in S3M representations via minimal pairs. We introduce prosodic ABX, an extension of this framework to evaluate prosodic contrast with only a handful of examples and no explicit labels. Also, we build and release a dataset of English and Japanese minimal pairs and use it along with a Mandarin dataset to evaluate contrast in English stress, Japanese pitch accent, and Mandarin tone. Finally, we show that model and layer rankings are often preserved across several experimental conditions, making it practical for low-resource settings.

items.title: Phonetic Error Analysis of Raw Waveform Acoustic Models
items.authors: Erfan Loweimi(Cisco; University of Edinburgh); Zhengjun Yue(Chinese University of Hong Kong); Andrea Carmantini(University of Edinburgh); Zoran Cvetkovic(KCL); Steve Renals(University of Edinburgh); Peter Bell(University of Edinburgh)
items.abstract: We analyse error patterns of raw waveform acoustic models on TIMIT phone recognition beyond the overall phone error rate (PER). PER is decomposed across three broad phonetic class(BPC) categorisations, and confusion matrices are constructed from substitution errors. Our models combine parametric (SincNet, Sinc2Net) or non-parametric CNNs with Bidirectional LSTMs, achieving 13.9%/15.3% PER on Dev/Test, the best reported results for raw waveform models on TIMIT. Transfer learning from WSJ reduces PER to 11.3%/12.3%, surpassing the Filterbank baseline. Per-BPC analysis reveals that BLSTM layers benefit transition-dependent classes most, while WSJ transfer learning improves consonants roughly three times more than vowels. Confusion patterns are consistent across raw waveform and Filterbank systems, indicating that the dominant confusions reflect inherent phonetic similarities.

items.title: Beyond Semantic Dominance: Cognitive Affective Reasoning and Empathetic Response Alignment in Audio Language Models
items.authors: Zhixian Zhao(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Shuiyuan Wang(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Wenjie Tian(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Jingbin Hu(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Ziyu Zhang(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Lei Xie(Northwestern Polytechnical University)
items.abstract: While Audio Language Models (ALMs) demonstrate strong semantic understanding, they struggle with complex affective interactions. Specifically, textual semantic dominance often overshadows acoustic nuances, and a lack of cognitive depth leads to generic, emotion-agnostic responses. We propose CogAudio-LLM, a novel cognitive affective reasoning framework. To mitigate semantic dominance, we build LIME-440K, a "lexically-identical, multi-emotion" dataset designed to facilitate acoustic-semantic decoupling. We introduce EIPS, a 4-step Chain-of-Thought (CoT) mechanism incorporating psychological reasoning. For inference efficiency, multi-stage training explicitly establishes EIPS via supervised fine-tuning, then distills this logic into an implicit generation process. Finally, we design DR-SAPO (Dual-Route Soft Adaptive Policy Optimization) to dynamically balance the logical rigor of the CoT with the empathetic quality of the direct response.

items.title: AudioGround: Fine-Grained Temporal Grounding in Audio via Deterministic Boundary Supervision
items.authors: Mingi Kim(Chung-Ang University); Minchol Kwon(Chung-Ang University); Junyeong Kim(Chung-Ang University)
items.abstract: Current Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) can describe the sounds present in audio but cannot localize their occurrence-a critical gap for applications. Prior efforts to add temporal reasoning either rely solely on coarse multi-choice distinctions or depend on LLM-inferred timestamps whose accuracy is unverifiable. We address this with a time-aware audio instruction-tuning dataset, AudioGround-IT, that provides deterministic boundary supervision, yielding 49.9K instructions over 835 hours of audio across four temporal tasks. To leverage this supervision for temporal grounding in LALMs, we propose AudioGround, a lightweight extension of SALMONN that uses a sliding-window Q-Former to compress encoder features and receives timestamp conditioning and absolute time embeddings. Evaluations on multiple temporal grounding benchmarks show that AudioGround substantially outperforms prior LALMs, demonstrating that deterministic boundary supervision transfers effectively to real-world audio.

items.title: A Closer Look at Failure Modes in Temporal Understanding of Large Audio-Language Models
items.authors: Apoorva Kulkarni(University of Maryland ); Kaousheik Jayakumar(University of Maryland ); Sreyan Ghosh(University of Maryland ); Sarah Wiegreffe(University of Maryland ); Dinesh Manocha(University of Maryland ); Ramani Duraiswami(University of Maryland )
items.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) achieve strong performance on a variety of audio understanding tasks but continue to struggle with temporal reasoning, a fundamental capability central to human auditory perception. Understanding the causes of these failures remains challenging as existing benchmarks report performance gaps without probing underlying mechanisms. To address this, we introduce a benchmark with 1,657 questions across three foundational tasks designed specifically for mechanistic analysis. Examining model outputs across varying input settings (behavioral analysis) reveals that models often under-utilize audio when textual cues are available. We also provide the first causal mechanistic analysis of temporal reasoning failures in LALMs. Comparing attention upweighting against scaling, we find that redistributing attention across audio tokens is more effective than increasing audio attention. Targeting task-relevant tokens yields further gains. These findings suggest that modality imbalance alone cannot explain failures. Attention scaling at bottleneck layers improves accuracy from 55.9% to 59.1% without fine-tuning, demonstrating a promising direction for future work.

items.title: Towards Deep Contextual Reasoning from Broad Descriptions for ASR with Speech-LLM via Metadata-Driven Reasoning Chains
items.authors: Jakob Poncelet(KU Leuven); Hugo Van hamme(KU Leuven)
items.abstract: Speech recognition often fails on rare, domain-specific terms and context-related named entities. Existing contextualization techniques typically bias decoding with keywords or phrase lists, which does not scale well or exploit deeper knowledge. We propose a training method that teaches a speech-LLM to use broad descriptions (e.g. from videos) as weak semantic priors to perform contextual reasoning grounded in the audio. We build 400 hours of reasoning-augmented speech data by pairing erroneous hypotheses with video metadata and LLM-generated reasoning explanations that justify context-driven corrections. We finetune the speech-LLM to perform chain-of-thought reasoning: generate an initial transcript, then reason over the context, and finally return a corrected transcript. On held-out YouTube-derived test sets, our approach reduces errors, with specific improvements on rare words and named entities, and lays groundwork for deeper contextual reasoning in speech recognition.

items.title: Entity Binding Failures in Speech LLM Reasoning: Diagnosis and Chain-of-Thought Intervention
items.authors: Ming-Hao Hsu(CUHK-Shenzhen); Xiaohai Tian(ByteDance); Jun Zhang(ByteDance); Zhizheng Wu(CUHK-Shenzhen)
items.abstract: Speech Large Language Models (SLLMs) underperform their text counterparts on complex reasoning. We reveal that this gap is not a uniform cognitive deficit. Evaluating two architecturally diverse SLLMs, we show speech-to-text (S2T) remains comparable to text-to-text (T2T) on spatial, syntactic, and factual tasks. Yet on logical tasks requiring entity tracking, S2T accuracy collapses to chance. We diagnose this as an entity binding failure: continuous speech features blur precise entity-property associations during implicit reasoning. To validate this diagnosis, we introduce Entity-Aware Chain-of-Thought (EA-CoT), a lightweight inference-time intervention forcing SLLMs to enumerate entities and bind them to claims before reasoning. EA-CoT bridges the gap, even when spoken names are misrecognized, yielding up to a 24.4 percentage-point accuracy gain. Ablations confirm the gains stem from explicit semantic binding, reframing the gap as an elicitation failure rather than a missing capability.

items.title: Noise-Aware In-Context Learning for Hallucination Mitigation in ALLMs
items.authors: Qixuan Huang(JAIST); Khalid Zaman(JAIST); Masashi Unoki(JAIST)
items.abstract: Auditory Large Language Models (ALLMs) show strong performance in audio understanding and reasoning, but their reliability is limited by hallucinations. Existing evaluation methods cast hallucination detection as binary classification, failing to capture the nuanced patterns in generative audio tasks, while mitigation methods often rely on costly fine-tuning. To address this, we propose a plug-and-play Noise-Aware In-Context Learning (NAICL) method. NAICL constructs a noise prior library, retrieves noise examples relevant to the input audio, and incorporates them as contextual priors to reduce speculative associations and generate more conservatively when acoustic evidence is insufficient. We also establish the Clotho-1K hallucination benchmark, define four types of auditory hallucinations, and introduce fine-grained evaluation metrics. Experiments show that evaluated ALLMs share similar hallucination behaviors, and NAICL reduces the hallucination rate from 26.53% to 16.98%.

items.title: CoRE: Contrastive Evidence-Aware Rescoring for Multiple-Choice Audio Question Answering
items.authors: Peihong Zhang(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Zhixin Li(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Yuxuan Liu(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Yiqiang Cai(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Yizhou Tan(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Shengchen Li(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University)
items.abstract: Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) achieve strong performance on multiple-choice Audio Question Answering (AQA) but often exhibit modality bias, over-relying on textual priors in questions and candidate options rather than grounded acoustic evidence. We present CoRE, a training-free, plug-and-play test-time option re-scoring method. CoRE constructs counterfactual audio via chunk permutation and random segment reversal to disrupt long-range temporal structure while largely preserving short-time acoustics. It estimates option-level evidence gain by contrasting scores from original and counterfactual audio, and applies an adaptive evidence-aware gate for final prediction. Under a unified option-scoring protocol, experiments on DCASE 2025 Task 5 and AIR-Bench SoundQA show consistent gains with Qwen2-Audio and Kimi-Audio.

items.title: Silence is Golden: Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Audio-Language Models via Layer-Weighted Vector Steering
items.authors: Tsung-En Lin(National Taiwan University; ASUS Open Cloud Infrastructure Software Center,); Kuan-Yi Lee(National Taiwan University; ASUS Open Cloud Infrastructure Software Center,); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University; NTU AI-CoRE)
items.abstract: Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) excel in Audio QA but often suffer from hallucinations ungrounded in the audio. To our knowledge, we are the first to propose applying vector steering to the audio domain to mitigate this. Unlike text-based steering, our silence-anchored contrastive approach steers the model away from hallucinations by contrasting active audio against a silent baseline. Probing internal states reveals a strong correlation between specific layer representations and output correctness. Leveraging this, we introduce Layer-Weighted Vector Steering (LWVS), a training-free intervention that increases steering strength at influential layers. On the Audio Hallucination QA dataset, LWVS significantly outperforms baselines, boosting Recall on the Gemma model by 15.6% (53.4% to 69.0%). Crucially, MMAU benchmark tests confirm LWVS preserves and even enhances general audio understanding, achieving an 8% relative accuracy increase on the Qwen model (54.8% to 59.2%).

items.title: Search-GRT: Guided Retrieval Training of Search Agents to Optimize for Complex Question Answering
items.authors: Aounon Kumar(Samsung Electronics); Sudipta Paul(Samsung Electronics); Vivek Kulkarni(Samsung Electronics); Vijay Srinivasan(Samsung Electronics); Srinivas Chappidi(Samsung Electronics)
items.abstract: Streaming multi-speaker ASR is a challenging task that must balance accuracy, latency, and efficiency while handling overlapping speech and maintaining coherent longcontext modeling over extended conversations in an online fashion. We present a unified framework that categorizes streaming multi-speaker ASR into four architectural strategies based on how diarization and ASR are integrated. Using a shared pair of open-source streaming ASR and diarization models as a common foundation, we derive four multi-speaker ASR systems that differ in whether they employ multiple model instances, fine-tuning, or both. We evaluate these systems across multi-speaker accuracy, single-speaker accuracy degradation, memory footprint, and training complexity. Through this systematic architectural analysis, we clarify the design space for streaming multi-speaker ASR and provide practical guidance for selecting the most suitable approach under diverse deployment constraints.

items.title: Breaking Neutral Bias: Zero-Human-Annotation Fine-Grained Emotion Enrichment via Semantic Drift and Discriminative Re-ranking
items.authors: Qihang Lu(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Wenbing Yang(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Bingsong Bai(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Zihan Sun(Hello Group Inc.); Yueran Hou(Hello Group Inc.); Peilei Jia(Hello Group Inc.); Ya Li(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Jun Gao(Hello Group Inc.); Yingming Gao(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
items.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) suffer from Neutral Bias, failing to capture subtle emotional nuances. Existing attempts to address this through text augmentation usually introduce acoustic hallucinations. To address these issues without costly human annotation, we propose a data-centric paradigm: Semantic Drift and Discriminative Re-ranking. Our method employs an LLM to perform multi-dimensional semantic drift, exploring diverse emotional hypotheses beyond neutral baselines. Subsequently, a discriminative judge model filters drifted hypotheses via hard-negative contrastive learning, grounding them in raw acoustic signals. Experiments confirm this hypothesize-and-verify mechanism transforms coarse, neutral-biased labels into precise, acoustically grounded descriptions, enriching fine-grained emotional detail and downstream expressiveness.

items.title: Acoustic Pharyngometry as an Auditable Anchor for Cross-Speaker EMA Normalization
items.authors: Daniel Friedrichs(Zurich Forensic Science Institute; University of Zurich); Valeriia Vyshnevetska(University of Zurich)
items.abstract: Cross-speaker analyses of electromagnetic articulography (EMA) are confounded by vocal-tract morphology. We present an auditable palate-referenced normalization combining palate-length scaling with a pharyngometry-derived oral landmark anchoring a low-parameter anterior-posterior warp. In German diadochokinetic (DDK) sequences, interspeaker dispersion of multisensor tongue trajectories falls from 31.28 mm to 26.36 mm (scaling) and 26.13 mm (scaling+warp; 16.5% total; most from scaling). Yet leave-one-speaker-out ridge regression does not improve F1/F2 prediction from EMA for DDK or sustained vowels (Hz, Bark, tract-length-normalized). Speaker identification remains high for absolute positions but drops after removing static offsets, indicating residual speaker structure beyond a one-dimensional warp. The method improves geometric comparability but not speaker-independent articulatory-acoustic mapping.

items.title: Vocal Tract Disparity and Potential Implications for Speaker Recognition
items.authors: Tiena Danner(University of Neuchâtel); Valeriia Vyshnevetska( University of Neuchâtel; University of Zurich); Daniel Friedrichs(University of Zurich; Zurich Forensic Science Institute (FOR)); Steven Moran( University of Neuchâtel; University of Zurich)
items.abstract: Perceptual experiments show that listeners recognize female speakers with lower accuracy than male speakers. Automatic speaker recognition systems may also show performance bias against female speakers even when training data sets are gender balanced. The underlying reasons for this discrepancy are unclear. Here, we apply geometric morphometrics to quantify sex-related morphological vocal tract disparity – the extent of shape variation – across both resting and articulatory configurations. We find that male speakers exhibit greater disparity in both resting and articulatory configurations. This morphological idiosyncrasy may in turn generate more discriminable acoustic signatures and offer a biological explanation for higher recognition accuracies for male voices by humans and machines. Our results suggest that innate variation in vocal tract morphology may contribute to performance bias in voice technology and voice perception by human listeners.

items.title: Towards Language-Agnostic Speech Inversion
items.authors: Saba Tabatabaee(University of Maryland College Park); Mark Tiede(Yale University); Suzanne Boyce(University of Cincinnati); Liran Oren(University of Cincinnati); Carol Espy-Wilson(University of Maryland College Park)
items.abstract: Characteristic timing patterns are reflected in the acoustic speech signal, encompassing both vocal tract configuration and acoustic excitation. Previous studies have demonstrated that speech inversion (SI) systems can recover these timing patterns from speech, including oral tract variables (tongue and lip constrictions) and source information such as periodic and aperiodic energies and fundamental frequency. In this study, we develop an SI system that simultaneously estimates oral tract variables and three source information parameters trained on co-recorded American English speech audio and articulatory kinematics and investigate cross-linguistic generalizability by evaluating performance on previously unseen languages. Pearson product-moment correlation scores of 0.83 and 0.74 were achieved on untrained French and Russian respectively, across oral tract variables and source information when comparing estimated data with ground-truth measurements.

items.title: Influence of Vocal Tract Curvature on Speech Acoustics: A Three-Dimensional FEM Analysis
items.authors: Debasish Ray Mohapatra(University of British Columbia); Sidney Fels(University of British Columbia)
items.abstract: Vocal tract curvature influences speech acoustics by shifting formant frequencies and exciting higher-order transverse modes. Nevertheless, many physics-based acoustic models approximate the vocal tract as a straight three-dimensional (3D) tube with a varying cross-sectional area. Although wave propagation in realistic vocal tract geometries has been studied previously, the specific effects of tract curvature on resonance frequencies remain largely unexplored. In this study, a 3D finite element (FE) wave solver is employed to characterize the frequency response of curved vocal tracts up to 14 kHz. The degree of curvature is systematically varied for vocal tracts with both uniform and non-uniform cross-sectional areas. For uniform cross-sections, curvature has a negligible effect on the frequency response. In contrast, for non-uniform cross-sections, curvature excites higher-order transverse modes at high frequencies and produces noticeable formant shifts above 10 kHz.

items.title: Morphoacoustic Modeling of a Dynamic 3D Vocal Tract Using MRI-Constrained Deformations and FEM Acoustics
items.authors: Tharinda Piyadasa(University of Sydney); Michael Proctor(Macquarie University); Tünde Szalay(University of Sydney); Joan Glaunès(Université Paris Cité); Amelia Gully(University of York); Kirrie Ballard(University of Sydney); Emily Kiff(University of York); Naeim Sanaei(Westmead Hospital); Sheryl Foster(University of Sydney; Westmead Hospital); David Waddington(University of Sydney); Craig Jin(University of Sydney)
items.abstract: Understanding the dynamic relationship between 3D vocal tract geometry and speech acoustics is central to speechproduction modelling. Using a constrained Large Deformation Diffeomorphic Metric Mapping (LDDMM) framework, we combine volumetric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of sustained vocal tract postures with midsagittal real-time MRI of short coarticulated utterances to construct dynamic 3D vocal tract models with time-varying acoustic responses. We demonstrate the approach on an [5ô5] utterance by an Australian English speaker. Five acoustic landmarks define evaluation states in the reference recording, and intermediate meshes are sampled from an rtMRI-parametrised deformation trajectory constrained by midsagittal contours. Finite-element simulations estimate formants from the resulting geometries. Simulated formants are systematically higher, yet track the reference formant trajectories, consistent with hyperarticulation in sustained speech produced under noisy conditions.

items.title: An Approach to Simultaneous Acquisition of Real-Time MRI Video, EEG, and Surface EMG for Articulatory, Brain, and Muscle Activity During Speech Production
items.authors: Jihwan Lee(University of Southern California); Parsa Razmara(University of Southern California); Kevin Huang(University of Southern California); Sean Foley(University of Southern California); Aditya Kommineni(University of Southern California); Haley Hsu(University of Southern California); Woojae Jeong(University of Southern California); Prakash Kumar(University of Southern California); Xuan Shi(University of Southern California); Yoonjeong Lee(University of Southern California); Tiantian Feng(University of Southern California); Takfarinas Medani(University of Southern California); Ye Tian(University of Southern California); Sudarsana Reddy Kadiri(University of Southern California); Krishna Nayak(University of Southern California); Dani Byrd(University of Southern California); Louis Goldstein(University of Southern California); Richard M. Leahy(University of Southern California); Shrikanth Narayanan(University of Southern California)
items.abstract: Speech production is a complex process spanning neural planning, motor control, muscle activation, and articulatory kinematics. While the acoustic speech signal is the most accessible product of the speech production act, it does not directly reveal its causal neurophysiological substrates. We present the first simultaneous acquisition of real-time (dynamic) MRI, EEG, and surface EMG, capturing several key aspects of the speech production chain: brain signals, muscle activations, and articulatory movements. This multimodal acquisition paradigm presents substantial technical challenges, including MRI-induced electromagnetic interference and myogenic artifacts. To mitigate these, we introduce an artifact suppression pipeline tailored to this tri-modal setting. Once fully developed, this framework is poised to offer an unprecedented window into speech neuroscience and insights leading to brain-computer interface advances. The source code and data are available.

items.title: The ArtComp dataset: Articulatory and Acoustic Measurements of Swedish in Speech with Naturally Manipulated Jaw Position
items.authors: Elísabet Eir Cortes(Stockholm University); Lisa Gustavsson(Stockholm University); Ellen Marklund(Stockholm University)
items.abstract: The ArtComp dataset contains time-aligned articulatory and acoustic data from seven native speakers of Central Standard Swedish (CSS). Articulatory data consist of electromagnetic articulography (EMA), electroglottography (EGG) and video. Acoustic data consist of analysis output from high quality audio recordings. The dataset is unique in that it consists of speech where jaw position is perturbed by natural means. Variable vocal effort ranging from soft to shouting was elicited, resulting in variable and exaggerated jaw opening. This type of data enables research targeting adaptive behaviour in the other articulators. Methods used in collecting and post-processing this dataset are described in detail, together with rationale for the methods chosen. A preview of data is given as time-variations and 2D-tracings of sensor data, to visually illustrate processed data.

items.title: Articulatory Analysis of the Mandarin Alveolar–Retroflex Contrast Using Real-Time MRI
items.authors: Qi Wu(University of Tsukuba); Tatsuya Kitamura(Konan University)
items.abstract: This study uses real-time magnetic resonance imaging (rtMRI) to quantify articulatory correlates of the Mandarin alveolar-retroflex contrast. Air-tissue boundaries were extracted using grid-based vocal tract tracking, yielding four measures: normalized constriction location, constriction length, front cavity, and back cavity. Results showed robust retroflex effects on constriction location and front cavity, indicating consistent posterior displacement and systematic anterior cavity expansion. Constriction length effects were less consistent, and back cavity weakly discriminated consonant class. rtMRI frames further revealed frequent tongue-tip-down postures for retroflex tokens. Overall, constriction location and anterior cavity expansion emerged as stable correlates of the contrast, suggesting articulatory targets that may inform pronunciation instruction.

items.title: Tongue-Shape Strategies for Standard Mandarin Retroflex Sibilants: A Preliminary Ultrasound and Unsupervised Clustering Study
items.authors: Zixi Jing(University of Auckland); C. T. Justine Hui(University of Auckland); Karen Huang(University of Auckland); Catherine I. Watson(University of Auckland)
items.abstract: Standard Mandarin retroflex sibilants are often described as non-prototypical retroflexes and may show diverse articulatory realisations. Using tongue ultrasound imaging, we examined five female native speakers from diverse regional backgrounds producing rhyme-matched alveolar-retroflex sibilant minimal pairs in a carrier sentence. Tongue contours were extracted from target frames, represented as 42 points, and aligned by centroid centring. Unsupervised clustering of contour-based shape descriptors yielded six clusters, which were consolidated into three super-strategies (domed, humped, and concave), in a scheme that differs from prior descriptive frameworks. Compositional clustering of super-strategy proportions revealed systematic between-speaker differences. Overall, consistent with prior work, Standard Mandarin retroflex sibilants permit multiple tongue-shape strategies, and speakers show strong, speaker-specific preferences that group them into stable clusters.

items.title: BEST-RQ-2: Contextualize-Then-Predict, a Two-Step Approach for Self-Supervised Audio Representations
items.authors: Ludovic Tuncay(Université de Toulouse); Étienne Labbé(Université de Toulouse); Thomas Pellegrini(Université de Toulouse)
items.abstract: Self-supervised learning enables audio representations that transfer across domains and tasks. We present BEST-RQ-2, an evolution of BEST-RQ that retains frozen random-projection-based discrete targets while introducing a two-step contextualize-then-predict pretraining scheme. A ViT context encoder processes only the unmasked spectrogram regions, and a lightweight predictor infers targets for the masked regions; the predictor is discarded after pretraining. Replacing the original Conformer encoder with a ViT shifts performance across domains, slightly reducing speech performance while improving music and environmental sounds, with comparable average scores. The main improvement comes from decomposing masked prediction into separate contextualization and prediction stages. On the X-ARES and XARES-LLM benchmarks, BEST-RQ-2 consistently outperforms one-stage baselines in overall transfer while keeping inference compute unchanged. Code and model checkpoints are publicly available.

items.title: WQ-Fusion: Dynamic Gated Attention for Cross-Domain Audio Representation
items.authors: Mingda Lin(Wuhan University); Lei Ding(Wuhan University); Xinyue Zhou(Wuhan University); Tiantian Xiong(Wuhan University); Hanchen Pei(Wuhan University); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); Hao Zhang(Tencent AI Lab Seattle); Jingdong Chen(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Jacob Benesty(University of Quebec)
items.abstract: While pre-trained models excel in specialized tasks, learning universal representations across diverse acoustic domains remains challenging. To address this, we propose WQ-Fusion, a robust dual-encoder framework for cross-domain audio representation learning. Overcoming the limitations of static concatenation, WQ-Fusion integrates whisper and qwen via an Adaptive Feature Modulation module and a novel element-wise gated attention mechanism. This design enables dynamic feature selection, allowing the model to selectively emphasize relevant acoustic and semantic dimensions. Extensive experiments on the Interspeech 2026 Audio Encoder Capability Challenge (Track A) benchmark demonstrate that by effectively routing heterogeneous information, WQ-Fusion achieves a superior overall score of 0.836, significantly outperforming the strongest single-encoder baseline.

items.title: The Interspeech 2026 Challenge on Transfer of Pragmatic Intent in Speech-to-Speech Translation
items.authors: Nigel G. Ward(University of Texas at El Paso); Marcel de Korte(University of Texas at El Paso); Javier Vazquez(University of Texas at El Paso); Montserrat G. Molina(University of Texas at El Paso); Vanessa Bolado(University of Texas at El Paso); Carol Figueroa(University of Texas at El Paso); Eliya Nachmani(Ben Gurion University); John E. Ortega(Northeastern University); Satoshi Nakamura(Chinese University of Hong Kong)
items.abstract: The Interspeech 2026 challenge task on Transfer of Pragmatic Intent in Speech-to-Speech Translation was motivated by the fact that current speech-to-speech translation systems do not prioritize pragmatic fidelity, and thus do not ideally support people conversing across languages. This paper describes the design, datasets, and evaluation methods for the challenge, and the results for the submissions. We find that even the best system lags human performance by 1.2 points on a 5-point scale, and note strengths and weaknesses of our evaluation methods.

items.title: BiMamba2 Masked Discrete-Unit Prediction for Multilingual Speech Representation for Unsupervised Speech in the Wild Challenge
items.authors: Prakriti Subedi(Howard University); Howard Prioleau(Howard University); Saurav Aryal(Howard University)
items.abstract: We describe our submission to the Unsupervised Speech in the Wild (UPS) Challenge at Interspeech 2026, a bidirectional Mamba-2 (BiMamba2) encoder trained with masked discrete-unit prediction following the HuBERT-style paradigm. The 47.88M-parameter model is trained on 250 hours of speech across 67 languages from the MLCommons Unsupervised People's Speech dataset, with no labeled data. The objective combines masked k-means pseudo-label prediction with language identification supervision and VICReg regularization. On official evaluation, the system achieves an Adjusted Rand Index of 0.735, exceeding four baselines on speaker clustering. Language identification macro-F1 (0.073) and character error rate (0.870) remain below supervised baselines. We analyze a local–official discrepancy in metric scale and checkpoint ranking, highlighting limitations of in-distribution diagnostics for predicting Dynabench probe outcomes.

items.title: Content–Speaker Trade-offs in Continued Self-Supervised Pre-Training Across SSL Paradigms for Multilingual Speech
items.authors: Danner Schlotterbeck(Factored AI); Alessandro Huaman(Factored AI); Juan Gomez(Factored AI)
items.abstract: Continued pre-training (CPT) of self-supervised learning (SSL) models uses domain-specific unlabeled audio to improve downstream performance. However, existing work focuses on contrastive architectures, leaving discrete-unit models underexplored, and rarely examines catastrophic forgetting in multi-task setups. To bridge this gap, we study CPT across three SSL architectures on subsets of the MLCommons Unsupervised People's Speech dataset across three tasks. Re-computing pseudo-labels on target data and resuming masked prediction improves content tasks in label-scarce domains, though gains are high-variance across seeds and data scale. In contrast, comparing discrete-unit and contrastive models reveals a systematic trade-off: CPT degrades speaker-discriminative information in discrete-unit models, an effect contrastive models do not exhibit. These findings highlight undocumented task specialization patterns under CPT, serving as a reference for future domain adaptation.

items.title: Unsupervised Speech in the Wild Challenge: Learning Robust Multilingual Representations
items.authors: Rafael Mosquera Gómez(Factored AI; MLCommons); Juan Felipe Rodríguez(Factored AI); Daniel Galvez(Nvidia); Sarah Luger(MLCommons)
items.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has achieved remarkable progress in speech representation learning, yet most models are pretrained on comparatively curated corpora with limited acoustic variability. We introduce the Unsupervised Speech in the Wild (UPS) 2026 Challenge, a benchmark designed to evaluate representation learning under large-scale, heterogeneous web audio conditions. Participants are restricted to pre-train from scratch or continue pretraining from a checkpoint using Unsupervised People's Speech (UPS) dataset, comprising over 800,000 hours of publicly licensed web audio, with approximately 522,000 hours of detected speech, and are evaluated on three complementary tasks: language identification, few-shot automatic speech recognition, and speaker clustering.

items.title: Beyond Acoustic Sparsity and Linguistic Bias: A Prompt-Free Paradigm for Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis
items.authors: Haopeng Geng(The University of Tokyo); Longfei Yang(The University of Tokyo); Xi Chen(The University of Tokyo); Haitong Sun(The University of Tokyo); Daisuke Saito(The University of Tokyo); Nobuaki Minematsu(The University of Tokyo)
items.abstract: Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis (MDD) requires modeling fine-grained acoustic deviations. However, current ASR-derived MDD systems often face inherent limitations. In particular, CTC-based models favor sequence-level alignments that neglect transient mispronunciation cues, while explicit canonical priors bias predictions toward intended targets. To address these bottlenecks, we propose a prompt-free framework decoupling acoustic fidelity from canonical guidance. First, we introduce CROTTC, an acoustic model enforcing monotonic, frame-level alignment to accurately capture pronunciation deviations. Second, we implicitly inject mispronunciation information via the IF strategy under the knowledge transfer principle. Experiments show CROTTC-IF achieves a 71.77% F1-score on L2-ARCTIC and 71.70% F1-score on the Iqra'Eval2 leaderboard. With empirical analysis, we demonstrate that decoupling acoustics from explicit priors provides highly robust MDD.

items.title: IQRA 2026: Interspeech Challenge on Automatic Assessment Pronunciation for Modern Standard Arabic (MSA)
items.authors: Yassine El Kheir(DFKI & Technical University of Berlin); Amit Meghanani(University of Sheffield); Mostafa Shahin(University of New South Wales); Omnia Ibrahim(Alexandria University); Shammur Absar Chowdhury(QCRI); Nada AlMarwani(Taibah University); Youssef Elshahawy(HUMAIN); Ahmed Ali(HUMAIN)
items.abstract: We present the findings of the second edition of the IQRA Interspeech Challenge, a challenge on automatic Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis (MDD) for Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). Building on the previous edition, this iteration introduces Iqra_Extra_IS26, a new dataset of authentic human mispronounced speech, complementing the existing training and evaluation resources. Submitted systems employed a diverse range of approaches, spanning CTC-based self-supervised learning models, two-stage fine-tuning strategies, and using large audio-language models. Compared to the first edition, we observe a substantial jump of 0.28 in F1-score, attributable both to novel architectures and modeling strategies proposed by participants and to the additional authentic mispronunciation data made available. These results demonstrate the growing maturity of Arabic MDD research and establish a stronger foundation for future work in Arabic pronunciation assessment.

items.title: A Fusion-Aware Two-Stage Framework for Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis in Low-Resource Modern Standard Arabic
items.authors: Jing Yang(Wuhan University); Shuqing Zhang(Wuhan University); Yongyi Deng(Wuhan University); Pan Li(Wuhan University); Ting Dang(University of Melbourne); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); Jingdong Chen(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Jacob Benesty(University of Quebec)
items.abstract: Accurate phoneme recognition is pivotal for mispronunciation detection and diagnosis (MDD) in modern standard Arabic (MSA), yet remains constrained by data scarcity and the synthetic-real domain gap. This work proposes a two-stage end-to-end framework. It integrates a pre-trained encoder with causal dilated temporal convolutional networks to preserve fine-grained phonetic variations. A hierarchical two-stage strategy first learns general mappings from native/synthetic corpora, then adapts to scarce real learner data to mitigate domain shift without over-correction. Prediction stability is further enhanced via multi-checkpoint ensemble inference with N-gram rescoring. Evaluated on the QuranMB.v2 test set, our system achieves an F1-score of 0.7201, a 63.1% relative improvement over baseline (0.4414). This performance ranks at the top of the IqraEval.2 Challenge, establishing a new state-of-the-art for low-resource MSA in MDD.

items.title: The Interspeech 2026 NeckVibe Challenge: Voice Disorder Detection via Real-World Monitoring of Neck-Surface Vibration
items.authors: Ahmed Yousef(Massachusetts General Hospital; Harvard Medical School); Robert Hillman(Massachusetts General Hospital; Harvard Medical School); Jarrad Van Stan(Massachusetts General Hospital; Harvard Medical School); Matías Zañartu(Universidad Técnica Federico Santa María); Hamzeh Ghasemzadeh(Massachusetts General Hospital; University of Central Florida); Ben Kevelson(Massachusetts General Hospital); Daryush Mehta(Massachusetts General Hospital; Harvard Medical School)
items.abstract: Brief clinic voice disorder assessments miss daily voice use. As an Interspeech 2026 data challenge (NeckVibe), we released a large-scale dataset for vocal hyperfunction (VH) detection, with customized ambulatory hand-crafted voice features. The dataset was recorded during one week of daily activities using a smartphone system that captured neck skin-surface vibration via an accelerometer—including 582 individuals with VH and healthy controls contributing 46,400 monitored hours. For phonotraumatic VH detection, all teams exceeded baseline (AUC = 0.82), with the best test AUC = 0.93. Nonphonotraumatic VH detection was harder: four teams exceeded baseline (AUC = 0.78), with the best AUC = 0.86. Top methods used within-day variability, nonlinear models (XGBoost/CatBoost), speech–singing cues, and feature-to-feature ratios. The challenge yielded new insights into ambulatory VH monitoring for real-world assessment and personalized voice management.

items.title: Temporal Partitioning of Vocal Activity for Detecting Vocal Hyperfunction from Neck-Surface Accelerometer Data
items.authors: Łukasz Łazarski(Samsung R&D Institute); Bartłomiej Eljasiak(Samsung R&D Institute); Szymon Szmajdziński(Samsung R&D Institute); Teresa Makuch(Samsung R&D Institute); Iwan Ryżenkow(Samsung R&D Institute); Anna Plęs(Samsung R&D Institute); Władysław Średniawa(Samsung R&D Institute)
items.abstract: This study presents an ensemble-based framework for classifying Phonotraumatic (PVH) and Non-Phonotraumatic Vocal Hyperfunction (NPVH) using long-term neck-surface accelerometer data. A key factor in enhancing performance was the implementation of temporal data segmentation focused on specific periods of daily vocal activity. Models were developed using the NeckVibe Challenge dataset, comprising 582 individuals, including PVH/NPVH patients and matched healthy controls. On the official challenge test set, our ensemble solution for PVH detection achieved an AUC of 0.925, securing 1st place. Furthermore, our NPVH model reached an AUC of 0.820, significantly surpassing baseline and SOTA benchmarks. These findings underscore the role of feature engineering and temporal optimization in advancing machine learning for ambulatory healthcare. This work was part of the NeckVibe Challenge, organized by the Vocal Hyperfunction Clinical Research Center.

items.title: A Hierarchical Feature Engineering Framework for Automated Classification of Phonotraumatic and Non-Phonotraumatic Vocal Hyperfunction
items.authors: June-Woo Kim(Wonkwang University; GIST); Kangwook Jang(KAIST); Minu Kim(KAIST); Hyunju Lee(GIST)
items.abstract: Ambulatory neck-surface acceleration enables non-invasive monitoring of vocal hyperfunction, yet robust biomarkers for its subtypes remain limited. This study investigates the NeckVibe Challenge dataset to distinguish phonotraumatic (PVH) and non-phonotraumatic (NPVH) from healthy controls. We propose a hierarchical feature engineering framework comprising: (i) static, (ii) dynamic, (iii) ratio-based, (iv) coupling features capturing source filter interactions. While univariate statistical analysis shows strong separability for PVH but limited significance for NPVH, our machine learning pipeline, tailored for high-dimensional feature integration, identifies that coupling features are crucial for both tasks. We achieve an AUC of 0.891 for PVH and 0.728 for NPVH, suggesting that while PVH is near-linearly separable, NPVH discrimination benefits from modeling non-linear feature interactions.

items.title: Attention-Based Multiple Instance Learning with Tabular Stacking for Ambulatory Detection of PVH and NPVH
items.authors: Kiran Yerpude(Seoul National University of Science and Technology; Medisensing); Seung Gyu Jeong(Seoul National University of Science and Technology; Medisensing); Seong-Eun Kim(Seoul National University of Science and Technology; Medisensing)
items.abstract: Phonotraumatic vocal hyperfunction (PVH) and non-phonotraumatic vocal hyperfunction (NPVH) are voice disorders that result from excessive laryngeal muscle activity. The PVH is associated with tissue lesions, while the NPVH refers to functional dysregulation without tissue damage. Ambulatory accelerometers enable the ecological assessment of daily voice behavior, which is noisy and variable. Our method consists of a tabular model at the subject level and a deep multiple instance learning (MIL) model with fixed-lengthwindows of frame-level features. The predictions of these two models are combined via a stacking ensemble method. The tabular model employs CatBoost with day-level features to account for long-term voice behavior, while the MIL model uses a 1D residual network with gated attention pooling to focus on relevant voice segments. The proposed method achieves an official test AUC of 0.891 for PVH (rank 3) and 0.861 for NPVH (rank 1) on the NeckVibe Challenge 2026.

items.title: Coco-VC: Degradation-Robust Streaming Voice Conversion System on the Listener Side
items.authors: Ryo Kato(SoftBank Corp.); Ryutaro Matsunaga(SoftBank Corp.); Toshio Imamura(SoftBank Corp.); Akinori Maeda(SoftBank Corp.); Shuhei Takahara(SoftBank Corp.); Shinnosuke Takamichi(The University of Tokyo; Keio University)
items.abstract: In telephone conversations, speakers lack the means to know how clearly their voice reaches the listener. This degradation in naturalness stems not only from the acoustic and communication environments but also from the speaker's unintelligible timbre. To address this issue, our real-time voice conversion (VC) system, Coco-VC, performs on the listener side. It is built with telephony data augmentation and multi-teacher distillation to extract robust representations. The interactive demonstration showcases a real-time, low-latency streaming VC on a standard laptop, allowing users to seamlessly switch VC settings via an intuitive GUI. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that Coco-VC maintains high quality even for degraded telephony speech compared to existing streaming VC systems.

items.title: Listening to Motion in Space: Vision-Grounded Event-wise Video-to-Audio Generation and Rendering
items.authors: Hyeonwoo Park(Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology); Dayeon Ku(Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology); Hong Kook Kim(Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology; AunionAI Co., Ltd.)
items.abstract: We present VisionSFX, a real-time, vision-grounded video-to-audio (V2A) workflow that generates editable, binaurally-rendered audio from silent video. Conventional V2A systems output a single mono mixture of all sources, which precludes the per-source editing and spatial control routinely required in film post-production, game engines, and AR/VR. End-to-end binaural systems can produce spatialized output but rely on large paired video-binaural training corpora. VisionSFX adopts a training-free route. A vision-language model first decomposes the scene into discrete sound events. Each event is generated independently by a pretrained V2A model within its own temporal window, while ambience is produced separately by a video-agnostic text-to-audio model. The resulting tracks are then spatialized post-hoc using optical-flow centroids with ego-motion correction, monocular depth, and binaural rendering. The pipeline requires no training, fine-tuning, or paired binaural data. Because each source is generated and stored separately, editing one-through re-prompting, repositioning, or timeline injection-leaves all others unchanged. At the booth, visitors upload a video clip and watch a per-source timeline populate within approximately one minute. They then drag sources around in 3D space, rewrite their prompts, or inject new events, with each change reflected on headphones in real time.

items.title: Automatic generation of audio comic from manga images
items.authors: Sota Koshino(Keio University); Shotaro Ueji(Keio University); Shinnosuke Takamichi(Keio University; National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology); Tomohiko Nakamura(National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology)
items.abstract: An audio comic is a derivative work based on manga augmented with voice acting. Our system provides a function that (semi-)automatically generates audio comics from manga images. In this paper, we report on the processing pipeline of the system and the objective and subjective evaluation results of the generated audio comics.

items.title: Programmable Speech Synthesis without Computers
items.authors: Takayuki Arai(Sophia University)
items.abstract: We present mechanical speech synthesis devices based on dynamic physical models of the human vocal tract. The models consist of a main vocal tract, with or without nasal branches. The configuration of the main tract is controlled by six sliding blocks inserted from the bottom. To control the position of each block, we tested two cam mechanisms: linear cams and rotating cams. In both cases, the cam profile determines the height of each block. Therefore, for each target phrase, the cam shapes must be redesigned. To make this process “programmable,” we developed a set of interchangeable plates with different profiles, allowing arbitrary cam shapes to be realized by inserting them into the base. This programmable approach allows the synthesis of multiple speech phrases using sliding-block-type vocal-tract models.

items.title: VoiceQualityGUI: A Tool for Word-Level Voice Quality Modifications
items.authors: Harm Lameris(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Alan Villamil(University of Texas at El Paso); Nigel G. Ward(University of Texas at El Paso)
items.abstract: Voice quality profoundly affects the perceived pragmatic function and suitability of synthesized speech. However investigation has lagged, due to the lack of tools for exploration. To address this need, we have developed a tool that supports modification of creakiness, breathiness, and nasality down to the word level, using an improved version of the VoiceQualityVC voice conversion system. Users can manipulate these properties and experience how such local modulations alter the perceived conversational meanings.

items.title: DsNA(Digital sigNature for Audios): A Unique Method to Fingerprint Audio Files Generated by Text to Speech
items.authors: Vishal Gourav(Oracle Corporation); Phanindra Mankale(Oracle Corporation)
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of text-to-speech (TTS) systems has enabled the large-scale generation of highly natural synthetic speech, raising critical concerns around audio provenance, authenticity, and misuse. In this work, we present DsNA (Digital sigNature for Audios), a lightweight post-generation fingerprinting framework designed to embed verifiable signatures directly into TTS-generated audio. Unlike traditional audio fingerprinting methods that rely on external matching or feature extraction, DsNA introduces a structured embedding mechanism in which a cryptographic signature derived from the audio and metadata is partitioned into shards and interleaved with segmented audio chunks. Preliminary evaluation demonstrates that the proposed method maintains audio fidelity, with no observable degradation in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) between original and fingerprinted audio. This paper discusses this idea, that enables intrinsic identification of generated speech while preserving signal quality.

items.title: Two Lessons Learned from the SGILE project: Efficient Building and Evaluation of TTS Voices
items.authors: Aidan Pine(National Research Council Canada); Korin Richmond(University of Edinburgh)
items.abstract: In line with the "Speaking Together" theme for Interspeech 2026, our Show & Tell showcases two contributions arising from recent work on the "Speech Generation for Indigenous Language Education" (SGILE) project. Both contributions facilitate building TTS voices for under-resourced languages: 1) the open-source EveryVoice TTS Toolkit can build high-quality voices using constrained amounts of audio data typical for under-resourced languages; 2) we have methodically evaluated speech evaluation techniques with the aim of maximising insights gained while minimising listener effort, especially important when few listeners are available. Our demo takes the form of a web app which combines both these aspects in a single interactive interface: users can experience first-hand a selection of EveryVoice TTS voices through a listening test design that has been little used in the speech synthesis field so far.

items.title: Scalable Audio Scene Generation with the Treble SDK
items.authors: Georg Götz(Treble Technologies); Konstantinos Gkanos(Treble Technologies); Steinar Guðjónsson(Treble Technologies); Daniel Gert Nielsen(Treble Technologies); Jesper Pedersen(Treble Technologies); Finnur Pind(Treble Technologies)
items.abstract: We present the Scene Generator of the Treble SDK, an interactive workflow for constructing realistic audio scenes from room-acoustic simulations, clean source material, and source or receiver definitions. The system supports controlled manual scene design as well as automated bulk generation. A scene is represented as a lightweight recipe containing tracks, source-to-impulse-response mappings, listener configuration, metadata, and target definitions. Audio is rendered only on demand, enabling fast inspection, serialisation, sharing, and scalable dataset generation. In the demonstration, participants build a multi-speaker conversational scene with background noise, visualise it as a timeline and 3D room view, render the scene, inspect targets and transcripts, and then generate many randomised scenes from compact rules.

title: Voice Quality Aspects of Speech
